14: # Theming a chart from DESIGN.md
15: 
16: ## 1. OVERVIEW
17: 
18: `DESIGN.md` is a style reference, not a chart form. The chart packet applies one locally available
19: v3 reference to a copy of an existing form; it does not extract a site, open a URL or change the
20: stock palette. Extraction belongs to `sk-design-md-generator`.
21: 
22: ---
23: 
24: ## 2. THE COMMAND
25: 
26: ```bash
27: node .skilled/skills/sk-design/sk-design-chart/scripts/apply-design-md.cjs \
28:   path/to/DESIGN.md --forms grouped-bars,daily-line --out scratch/themed
29: ```
30: 
31: Use `--all` instead of `--forms` to copy every form. `--scheme light|dark|both` selects which
32: ground receives the reference: `light` derives the light ground and keeps the stock dark chrome,
33: `dark` derives the dark ground and keeps the stock light chrome, and `both` derives both when the
34: reference declares dark support. If a reference is light-only, its dark half is the stock dark
35: chrome with series re-derived against it. `--tokens tokens.json` supplies the optional sibling
36: token inventory explicitly; otherwise a sibling `tokens.json` is used when present.
37: 
38: The input must be a local file. A URL is refused. The output directory is created only after every
39: chosen form has a complete derived palette and both theme validations have passed. There is no
40: force option.
41: 
42: ---
43: 
44: ## 3. WHAT THE PARSER READS
45: 
46: The parser follows the v3 headings rather than searching for arbitrary prose:
47: 
48: | Reference section | Required shape | Used for |
49: | --- | --- | --- |
50: | `## Tokens — Colors` | `Name`, `Value`, `Token`, `Role` table | Chrome roles, chromatic series and emphasis |
51: | `## Tokens — Typography` | First typeface heading and its immediate `Substitute` line | Body stack, and mono heading when the reference supplies one |
52: | `## Tokens — Spacing & Shapes` → `### Border Radius` | `Element`, `Value` table | The five chart corner rungs |
53: 
54: A missing heading, table or substitute is reported by name and stops the run. Six-digit colour
55: values are the usable rows; gradients are not silently turned into flat colours.
56: 
57: ---
58: 
59: ## 4. THE ROLE MAPPING
60: 
61: The mapping preserves the chart packet's role vocabulary and uses table order as prominence:
62: 
63: | Chart role | Selection |
64: | --- | --- |
65: | `surface` | The lightest colour whose role names a background, surface, canvas, ground, panel or fill |
66: | `ink` | The darkest text-role colour on the light ground, and the lightest text-role colour on the dark ground |
67: | `muted` | A text-role colour nearest the stock muted ratio that still clears the text gate |
68: | `rule` | The selected ink colour held at the stock dark-rule alpha |
69: | `series-1` through `series-4` | Chromatic table values that clear the mark gate, each taken verbatim, chosen greedily by hue distance from the hues already chosen so no two neighbours share a hue; a pair that is both under the separation ratio and within thirty degrees of hue is refused as one colour. When fewer than four clear, the table's own neutral text tones fill the remaining series darkest first, with the ink held back until last so it stays free for emphasis. No value is adjusted |

73: declared dark `DESIGN.md` theme, or a supported `darkMode` in `tokens.json`, supplies the dark
74: ground. Otherwise the stock dark surface, ink, muted value and alpha rule stay in place and only
75: the series are re-derived against that ground. No colour is borrowed from the three stock semantic
76: systems to fill a missing chromatic role.
77: 
78: The corner ladder uses the largest measured radius that does not exceed each stock rung. A rung
79: with no measured value below its ceiling becomes `0px`; it never grows a corner beyond the stock
80: ladder. The measured primary typeface precedes its substitute stack in every body declaration, and every declaration that already names a monospace face takes the reference's mono stack; the choice is by what the declaration is, not by where it sits. A
81: dedicated mono typeface is used when the reference supplies one; otherwise the primary stack is
82: used for the mono declarations as well.
83: 
84: A table colour counts as chromatic when its HSL saturation is at least 24 percent; below that it
85: is a neutral and can only serve the chrome roles or fill a missing series. The threshold keeps a
86: warm grey out of the series ladder while letting a muted brand hue in.

93: magnitude ramp with step and end gates of its own. A colour table does not supply such a ramp, so
94: the script never themes an ordered form: naming one is refused, and `--all` skips it with a note.

100: reference's own table to the shared roles as one derived system, so the delivery and the stock
101: palette agree where the mapping lands on the same value and differ where it has to choose one,
102: which is the larger part of the colour table. The corner ladder is what reproduces the stock

104: still the reference the corpus came from. The check holds the palette file against that reference

110: and pins each file by hash. Overriding is unchanged: pass any other `DESIGN.md` path, including one
111: `sk-design-md-generator` has just produced, and the script themes from that instead.

116:

118: A reference with nothing that small has said nothing about that rung and the corpus value stands,
119: the way an ordered form keeps the stock ramp when a colour table cannot supply one. It used to
120: collapse to zero instead, which squared every data mark, legend swatch and progress capsule in a
121: themed set and said nothing about having done so.
122:

124: swatch and pill and its 8.4 on the card, which is the stock ladder exactly; the 2px mark corner is
125: below anything it publishes, so the corpus value stands. What the floor costs is worth stating rather
126: than leaving to be discovered: a reference whose corners are all larger than the corpus rungs
127: contributes none of them.
128: 
129: Mapping by the reference's own element names instead — its `cards` row straight to the card rung —
130: was measured and rejected. It happens to agree with the floor for this reference, whose `cards` row
131: is 8.4px, and it disagreed for the one before it, which named a 4px card and would have handed the
132: rung a corner the stock ladder had deliberately not taken. The floor is the rule that reproduced the
133: stock ladder from both, which is the one property that says the default is still the reference the
134: corpus came from. It buys that property at the cost of a reference with larger corners contributing
135: fewer of them, and that is the right side of the trade.
136: 
137: ---
138: 
139: ## 7. GATES BEFORE WRITING
140: 
141: The thresholds come from `assets/style-reference/evilcharts/palettes.json` on every run. The applicator uses the shared
142: colour arithmetic module that the checker requires, so the same transfer curve, luminance and
143: rounding produce both results.
144: 
145: - `textOnSurface` applies to ink and muted.
146: - `markOnSurface` applies to all four series and emphasis.
147: - Any two series must differ by the separation ratio or by thirty degrees of hue.
148: - Every colour role must be a six-digit hex; the checker errors on anything else rather than skipping the gates.
149: - `emphasisAgainstFirstSeries` applies to emphasis against series 1.
150: - `rule` remains ungated by design, but a dark rule must be its theme's ink followed by a non-full alpha.
151: 
152: Every failure names the role, measured ratio, gate and nearest table colour that clears it. The
153: script prints `RESULT: FAILED` and writes no output on a failure. A pass prints one `MAPPING` line
154: per role for both grounds, then writes the selected form copies and ends with `RESULT: PASSED`.
155: 
156: ---
157: 
158: ## 8. WHAT CHANGES IN A DELIVERY
159: 
160: The writer changes only the two sentinel-marked palette regions, their provenance comments, the
161: font-family declarations and the light corner ladder inside the palette. `CHART_DATA`, `READOUT`,
162: `CURVE`, geometry, the chart identity and every other byte remain unchanged. Each block starts with
163: the same deterministic comment shape:
164: 
165: ```css
166: /* CHART_PALETTE:BEGIN system=design-md */
167: /* DESIGN.md provenance: path=path/to/DESIGN.md sha256=<64 hex> generator=1.4.0.0 */
168: ```
169: 
170: The dark block carries the matching comment directly under its begin marker. The input path is
171: the path supplied to the command, not a rewritten absolute path, and the hash is the SHA-256 of
172: the input file.
173: 
174: `check-corpus.cjs` keeps the stock source-equality branch for `neutral`, `ordered` and
175: `categorical`. For a `design-md` block it instead requires the provenance comment and checks the
176: inline values in both themes against the same gates. `--extra DIR` runs the file-level checks over
177: HTML deliveries outside the package without adding them to the catalog:
178: 
179: ```bash
180: node .skilled/skills/sk-design/sk-design-chart/scripts/check-corpus.cjs --extra scratch/themed
181: ```
182: 
183: That separation is the safety line: a themed copy can be accepted by evidence without putting

15: # Chart Template Contract
16: 
17: A template is one HTML file. It opens on a double click, with no install, no package manager and no build step, and it keeps working when the person who received it edits the numbers by hand.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: Both of those properties are load-bearing. The reader is a writer or an operations analyst rather than a developer, and the file has to survive being emailed to somebody who will open it on a laptop with no network.
24: 
25: ---
26: 
27: ## 2. THE DELIVERY UNIT
28: 
29: One file holds one chart. Inside it, the visible unit is a card with five parts in a fixed order.
30: 
31: | Part | Marker | What goes in it |
32: | --- | --- | --- |
33: | Headline | `data-chart-part="headline"` | A conclusion, not a chart type. "Revenue by plan" is a label. "Where we gained and where we bled" is an argument |
34: | Subtitle | `data-chart-part="subtitle"` | The legend and the time range, in a sentence |
35: | Figure | `data-chart-part="figure"` | The drawing itself |
36: | Footer | `data-chart-part="footer"` | The one-line finding in ink, separated from the figure by the rule |
37: | Source | `data-chart-part="source"` | The muted description line in the footer; where the numbers came from |
38: 
39: The fixed five are what make a chart legible with no caption around it. The headline rule is the highest-value writing rule in this packet: a reader who takes nothing but the top line should still have learned something. The footer is part of the card rather than a caption added around it: the finding tells the reader what to notice, and the source stays attached to that reading.
40: 
41: ### Gallery and delivery are different things
42: 
43: A delivery is one card in one file, and it is what reaches a user. A gallery is many cards on one page, used as a workbench for finding a form. Never hand over a gallery. It carries every other chart's demo data with the user's one real chart somewhere inside it.
44: 
45: ---
46: 
47: ## 3. THE FILE SKELETON
48: 
49: Copy the skeleton from `assets/style-reference/evilcharts/palette-sheet-neutral.html`, which is a working file that passes every check. The structure is:
50: 
51: ```
52: <!doctype html>
53: <html lang="en">
54: <head>
55:   <meta charset>, <meta name="viewport">, <title>
56:   <meta name="chart-template"     content="<id>">
57:   <meta name="chart-color-system" content="<system>">
58:   <style>
59:     /* CHART_PALETTE:BEGIN system=<system> */
60:     /* DESIGN.md provenance: path=<local path> sha256=<64 hex> generator=<version> */
61:     :root { every colour role and every corner rung, pasted from the palette source }
62:     /* CHART_PALETTE:END */
63: 
64:     /* CHART_PALETTE_DARK:BEGIN system=<system> */
65:     /* DESIGN.md provenance: path=<local path> sha256=<64 hex> generator=<version> */
66:     @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
67:       :root { every colour role again, pasted from the same source's dark values }
68:     }
69:     /* CHART_PALETTE_DARK:END */
70: 
71:     everything else, referring only to var(--chart-…)
72:   </style>
73: </head>
74: <body>
75:   the card: headline, subtitle, figure, footer with finding and source
76:   a table carrying data-chart-table
77:   <script>
78:     /* CHART_DATA:BEGIN */
79:     the numbers, and nothing else
80:     /* CHART_DATA:END */
81: 
82:     /* CHART_SERIES:BEGIN */
83:     one object per named series: key, label, token and paint classes
84:     /* CHART_SERIES:END */
85: 
86:     /* READOUT:BEGIN */
87:     label formatter, value formatter and datum-field key for a card-bearing form
88:     /* READOUT:END */
89: 
90:     /* CURVE:BEGIN */
91:     const CURVE = 'linear' | 'step' | 'monotone', with one-line rationale
92:     /* CURVE:END */
93: 
94:     the drawing code
95:   </script>
96: </body>
97: </html>
98: ```

The dark pair carries its own name for that reason: a second block under the light block's name would be the same sentinel twice, and then nothing can say which region a drifted value came from.
101: 
102: ### The type scale, as the compact card register
103: 
104: The visual pass moves the corpus to the compact register in the frozen shadcn examples: a title
105: that is easy to scan, a description that stays secondary, and 12px figure labels that remain
106: legible beside a data mark. The palette source publishes the projection under `typeScale`, the
107: `type-scale` family reads it from there, and a size outside it fails rather than becoming a
108: one-off guess. The two palette proof sheets keep their finer six-rung scale under `sheetRoles`.
109: 
110: | Role | Size | What is set in it |
111: | --- | --- | --- |
112: | headline | 16px | The card title, semibold and ink coloured |
113: | body | 14px | The page default and the card description |
114: | label/tick/note | 12px | Axis ticks, footer labels, tooltip rows, legend labels and compact in-figure notes |
115: | month strip | 10px | A month name in the calendar grid, where the year leaves a narrow strip |
116: | hero | 56px | The single headline number in `progress-single` |
117: | ring total | 34px | The total at the centre of `unit-ring` |
118: 
119: The values are measured from the frozen shadcn copy: the card header keeps title and description
120: together (`chart-area-interactive.tsx:157-164`), Cartesian labels use the compact chart text
121: register (`chart.tsx:63-69`), and the footer uses `text-sm`, `font-medium` and a muted second row
122: (`chart-line-linear.tsx:78-84`). The standalone files express those roles in CSS rather than in
123: Tailwind utilities, but the scale is the same decision.
124: 
125: The two departures remain deliberate. `progress-single` prints its hero figure at 56px and
126: `unit-ring` prints its ring total at 34px because each is the point of the chart rather than a
127: label on it. `calendar-grid` keeps its 10px month strip because a year of days leaves no room for
128: the full label rung.
129: 
130: ### The shadcn visual register
131: 
132: The corpus keeps the shadcn choices that survive the standalone-file constraint. The frozen line
133: examples remove both axis and tick lines, leave an 8px tick margin, draw a 2px line and turn point
134: dots off (`chart-line-default.tsx:56-74`). The frozen area examples are our measurement of what
135: shadcn ships: a vertical 0.8-to-0.1 gradient with 0.4 flat opacity for stacked areas
136: (`chart-area-gradient.tsx:72-112`), from which ours derive — the shipped single-area fade runs
137: 0.35 to 0.04 (`daily-line.html:137-138`) and the shipped stacked bands sit at 0.4 flat. The frozen
138: tooltip content uses a bordered, rounded, padded, shadowed card with muted labels and mono values
139: (`chart.tsx:190-259`), while the legend uses 8px squares with 2px corners and a 16px row gap
140: (`chart.tsx:290-322`).
141: 
142: The HTML projection is deliberately local: `--chart-surface`, `--chart-rule`, `--chart-muted`,
143: and the series tokens supply all paint; the card is positioned inside `.figure`; and the card reads
144: the form's `READOUT` block. The tooltip is never an SVG text layer. A keyed multi-series form gets
145: one centered HTML legend row below the plot, generated from `CHART_SERIES`, with one button chip per key.
146: 
147: Cartesian single-series forms use the first categorical series token for their primary mark. The
148: emphasis token is reserved for the highlighted mark. Unit grids, rings, ordered ramps and other
149: non-Cartesian forms keep their existing colour logic because their colour is carrying a different
150: question.
151: 
152: ### The geometry defaults ride beside the palette block
153: 
154: Every file carries one `GEOMETRY DEFAULTS` block, immediately after its dark palette block. It
155: records the five measurements every file in the corpus shares: the 720-unit drawing frame, the
156: pan floor, the card width, the card padding and the page padding.
157: 
158: The block is a written record rather than an indirection, and that is forced rather than chosen.
159: Neither place these numbers are used can read a custom property. A `viewBox` attribute takes a
160: number, and rule 14's floor is read out of the stylesheet as a literal by the check that
161: enforces it, so a `min-width` resolving through a variable would fail the rule it satisfies.
162: 
163: What the block deliberately does not carry is the frame height or the four plot insets. Those
164: are per-form, because a left inset is sized to the widest label a form actually carries, and
165: copying one form's inset into another buys uniformity by cutting a label off. A form that
166: departs from a shared value says why beside the value it uses instead.
167: 
168: `geometry-block` asserts it. Every chart form and every proof sheet has to carry the block and
169: every copy has to match the others byte for byte. The set is derived from the two directories
170: rather than listed, so a new form joins it by existing rather than by being remembered, and a
171: corpus where the block had been scattered over some files would fail rather than pass a count.

175: ## 4. HOW IT RECEIVES DATA
176: 
177: One named array at the top of the inline script, between the `CHART_DATA` sentinels, and everything below it renders. That is the whole contract, and it is the right one, because the person editing a delivered file is looking for the numbers and nothing else.
178: 
179: The data block holds literal values. It never fetches, never computes the numbers it is displaying and never reads the clock. A chart that changes on its own cannot be reviewed, because two screenshots of one file disagree and nobody can tell which is the bug.
180: 
181: ### The one exception, named
182: 
183: Two forms compute a value they display, and both are deliberate: the waterfall's closing
184: total and the stacked area's per-period total. Neither invents a number. Each is the sum
185: of values the reader can already see, computed beside them and auditable against them, and
186: in both cases typing the total by hand would create a second copy that drifts the first
187: time a step is edited.
188: 
189: That is the whole exception and it does not generalise. A computed value is allowed when it
190: is a total of the typed values, sits next to them, and would otherwise be a hand-kept
191: duplicate. Everything else belongs upstream, in the workbook or query the numbers came
192: from. That covers a rate, a share of an untyped denominator, a smoothed series, and any
193: value derived from another source. The test is whether a reader holding only the data block can check the figure. If
194: they cannot, the file is computing rather than displaying.
195: 
196: Everything else the drawing code derives is geometry or presentation, not data: an axis
197: ceiling, a tick ladder, a bar height, a formatted label. Those are how the numbers are
198: drawn, and they are not what this clause is about.
199: 
200: ### A named series owns one token
201: 
202: When a form carries more than one named stream, the streams sit in one `CHART_SERIES` block
203: beside `CHART_DATA`. Each object has a stable `key`, the label a reader sees, exactly one
204: `--chart-series-N` token and the CSS classes that paint that stream. The declaration is the one
205: source for the name-to-paint relationship; the index is still the position used by the data array,
206: but it is not allowed to become a second mapping kept somewhere else in the file.
207: 
208: The keyed forms are `bar-line-composed`, `grouped-bars`, `parallel-axes`, `population-pyramid`,
209: `stacked-area` and `stacked-bars`. `series-mapping` checks both sides: an entry with no token or
210: more than one token fails, and a class whose paint does not match its key fails. Ordered colour
211: steps, sign classes and other categorical ladders keep their existing indexed contract; they are
212: not named series merely because they use more than one colour.
213: 
214: ### A card carries its readout knobs
215: 
216: Every form with `data-chart-tooltip` carries one `READOUT` block beside its data. The block owns
217: three local decisions: `label` formats the card's labels, `value` formats its values and `key`
218: names the property of the datum passed to card registration that supplies the card's label. The
219: registration path reads the label as `READOUT.label(datum[READOUT.key])`. When a displayed label is
220: computed or the registration has no existing row object, the caller passes a small record with a
221: literal property matching `key`. The value formatter may preserve a value already rendered by the
222: form's fixed-comma `fmt`, which keeps derived strings such as a signed change readable while still
223: giving the card one local knob.
224: 
225: `number-format` asserts the block and its use. A tooltip without `READOUT`, a block without all
226: three fields, a card path that does not read `READOUT.label`, `READOUT.value` and
227: `READOUT.key` from the registered datum, or a path that builds an object with `[READOUT.key]` only
228: to read that same property back is an error.
229: 
230: ### A time path states its curve
231: 
232: Any form that draws a path over time declares one `CURVE` block beside its data. The value is one
233: of `linear`, `step` or `monotone`, and a one-line rationale sits beside it. `linear` is the
234: default for measured trends because it connects the observations without adding a shape they did
235: not record. `step` is for discrete states. `monotone` is for a series whose meaning has been
236: reviewed and whose smooth path must not overshoot its observations. `natural` is not a contract
237: value: it adds curvature without saying what the data means.
238: 
239: The path builder reads `CURVE` when it assembles its `d` attribute, so changing the declaration
240: changes the construction rather than only the prose around it. `curve-contract` checks the
241: sentinel, the allowed set, the rationale and the read by the path. The current time-path forms
242: are `bar-line-composed`, `daily-line`, `stacked-area` and the `orders-after-the-price-change`
243: delivery; each ships `linear` because each is a measured trend with finite gaps left visible.
244: 
245: ### A form declares what its marks do
246: 
247: Whether a figure adds dots, how it fills the space under a line, and whether its zero means
248: anything are decisions the paint code makes either way. A `MARKS` block beside the data states
249: them in words a check can hold against the paint: `points` is `none`, `sparse` or `all`; `fill` is
250: `none`, `gradient` or `flat`; `zero` is `baseline` or `meaningful`. A one-line why sits beside
251: them, and it is the only prose in the block, because a longer reading of the drawing is the second
252: description that goes stale first.
253: 
254: `sparse` marks the readings the sentence cites and nothing else, which is why `daily-line` and
255: `spark` carry one dot each rather than twenty-eight. `all` belongs to the forms whose reading *is*
256: the point: `scatter`, `dumbbell`, `distribution-strip` and `parallel-axes`. `meaningful` is
257: declared by one form, `waterfall`, because its steps are signed and its baseline separates a rise
258: from a fall. Every other form's zero is the floor its bars stand on.
259: 
260: The `mark-policy` family holds each word against the drawing, not just against the vocabulary. A
261: declared fade needs a gradient and a declared flat fill needs an opacity, and neither accepts the
262: other's paint. A zero is meaningful exactly when a reading falls below it. Points are held one way
263: only: a form promising marks has to draw them, while a form declaring `none` may still carry a
264: circle, because several forms place an invisible one purely as something a pointer can reach.
265: 
266: ### A level a reader measures against is declared
267: 
268: A target, an average or a threshold drawn across a plot is a claim about the data, not decoration,
269: so a form that can carry one says whether it does. Every form built on the corpus's one vertical
270: value scale and a drawn grid declares a `REFERENCE` list of `{ value, label, why }`; an empty list
271: draws nothing, and the drawing takes all three fields from the block rather than from a data field
272: of its own.
273: 
274: That set is narrower than "cartesian", deliberately. A form reading two scales at once cannot say
275: which one a chart-wide value belongs to, which rules out `bar-line-composed`. A form whose value
276: runs along the horizontal, or whose points each answer to their own axis, has no single level to
277: draw, which rules out `pick-times-by-depot` and `parallel-axes`. `spark` has the scale and no axis,
278: no labels and no grid, so a named rule across it would break the form. The line is dashed at the ink
279: colour so it is not mistaken for the grid, and its label is set at the right edge of the plot, above
280: the rule.
281: 
282: Two forms carry a line, and both carry it for the same reason: the headline is a claim about a
283: level, and the level is already in the data. `daily-line` declares the first week's average, which
284: nothing after day eleven reaches. The `orders-after-the-price-change` delivery declares the ten
285: days before the change, 184 against 140 after it, which is the "almost a quarter lower" its
286: headline states. The `reference-line` family holds the block, the three fields, the read by the
287: drawing, that the drawing appends a rule, and that the file styles it.
288: 
289: `bullet` is not a consumer, and the reason is worth stating because it looks like one. Its target
290: is per row, not per plot: four measures carry four different targets against four different scales,
291: and a chart-wide list cannot express that. Its target stays in its data.
292: 
293: ### When a form cannot honour the data it was given
294: 
295: A form is honest inside a documented shape, and two different things set that shape. The catalog
296: states how much data a form can carry: `scatter` past twenty points and `heat-matrix` past a
297: hundred cells each grow the frame and print one line naming the count and the ceiling. The palette
298: states how many colours a form has to give out, which is a harder ceiling because the file cannot
299: paint past it at all: `unit-ring`, `unit-grid`, `stacked-bars`, `treemap` and `stacked-area` each
300: draw the marks past that ceiling outside the encoding, in the rule colour, and print the same kind
301: of line. Seven forms in total.
302: 
303: The colour ceiling is worth stating separately, because reaching past it used to fail silently and
304: loudly at the same time. A class the stylesheet defines no fill for is not an unstyled mark; it is
305: a black one, because black is what an SVG paints when nothing says otherwise. So the group the
306: encoding could not carry came out as the strongest mark on the page, under a key that never named
307: it. Nothing in a green run said so.
308: 
309: A missing reading gets the same treatment: `bar-line-composed`, `daily-line`, `daily-range` and
310: `stacked-area` break the mark at the gap rather than drawing through it, and print how many
311: readings were left out.
312: 
313: A notice belongs in the figure when a reader looking at the picture would otherwise draw a
314: wrong conclusion from it, and it is not spread across every form for its own sake. A console
315: warning was the alternative and was rejected: the person the ceiling protects is reading a
316: chart, not a developer console.
317: 
318: ### An empty data block says so, on every form and every delivery
319: 
320: All twenty-nine forms carry the same guard, marked `CHART_EMPTY_NOTICE`,
321: above their drawing code. When the data block holds nothing readable, the file prints one line in
322: the middle of the frame and draws nothing else.
323: 
324: The deliveries carried no guard at all until the ground for exempting them was read rather than
325: repeated. The exemption said a delivery carries the notice of the form it was built from, and none
326: of the six did. A delivery is also the copy somebody edits, which makes it the copy most likely to
327: be handed an empty block. The only file this does not reach is a proof sheet, whose data block is
328: the palette it draws rather than a reading it displays.
329: 
330: This is the clearest case the rule above describes rather than a new rule. An empty frame and a
331: chart whose values are all zero look identical, so a reader shown an empty box has no way to
332: tell which one they are holding. The notice tells them.
333: 
334: Readability is what the guard tests, not length. A block whose entries all carry values that are
335: not finite numbers has length and still has nothing to draw, so it fires. One row does not fire
336: it. That distinction matters more than it looks: a guard written against `length` alone passes an
337: array of nulls straight through to a drawing that has nothing to draw, and a guard that coerces
338: before it tests reads `null` as zero and calls it a reading. The corpus already had the right
339: test, in the three time forms that break a line at a gap, and this guard uses the same one.
340: 
341: The notice is a text element inside the drawing, so a screen reader reaches it exactly as it
342: reaches the ceiling notices. Its wording is fixed rather than assembled from the data block, so
343: nothing a reader pastes into the file can reach the picture as text.
344: 
345: `empty-notice` asserts it on every run, and it asserts more than the sentinel. The guard has to
346: sit below the data block it reads, because a guard above it tests a name that is not defined yet,
347: and it has to carry the labelled block and the break that let it stop the drawing. A guard that
348: prints the notice and then draws anyway prints it over an empty frame, which is the picture the
349: notice exists to prevent.

353: ## 5. WHAT IT MAY DEPEND ON
354: 
355: Nothing.
356: 
357: No charting library, no web font, no icon set, no boundary data, no CDN of any kind. Marks are drawn as inline vector output by the file's own script.
358: 
359: This is stricter than it needs to be for the no-build-step property alone, and it is deliberate. A remote dependency keeps the file working only while the network is up and the host still exists, which turns "it opens on a double click" into "it opened on a double click in the office". The cost is real: each form is hand-drawn, and forms that genuinely need a layout engine, such as dense node-link networks, are out of the corpus rather than in it with a library attached.
360: 
361: The check enforces this by failing any remote `src` or `href`, any `@import` and any `fetch`, `XMLHttpRequest` or dynamic `import` in the file.

365: ## 6. WHERE COLOUR COMES FROM
366: 
367: A palette block is the only place in the file where a colour value appears. Everything else refers to `var(--chart-…)`.
368: 
369: Take the block from the corpus check: when a template's block is missing or has drifted, the failure message prints the exact block to paste. That is the whole workflow, and it is why there is no generation step. The dark block works the same way and prints the same way.
370: 
371: ### The second block answers a dark system
372: 
373: A file carries one palette block per theme and no more than two, each matched against its own projection of the palette source in both directions.
374: 
375: The second block sits inside the same style element, immediately after the light one, wrapped in a `prefers-color-scheme: dark` media query and its own sentinel pair. It redeclares the six colour roles and nothing else. The corner rungs stay in the light block alone, because a corner cannot differ between two grounds and a value copied into a second place is a value that can disagree with the first.
376: 
377: The delivered file still follows the reader's operating-system preference by default. For a
378: deterministic capture, it also accepts `?scheme=light` or `?scheme=dark` and sets
379: `data-scheme` on the document before the chart paints; the matching dark projection sits beside
380: the media query. The query exists because a capture on a dark machine has no other way to see the
381: light rendering: pinning `color-scheme` from outside does not change what `prefers-color-scheme`
382: resolves inside the document. A browser that
383: never resolves either signal paints the light block, and print still has the light document path.
384: 
385: Two blocks double the surface a drift can hide in, which is the cost of the amendment and the reason the ceiling is two rather than open. The check counts the sentinels and fails a third block, a repeated pair and a value that disagrees with the source in either direction.
386: 
387: To show a colour value as text, read it at runtime with `getComputedStyle(document.documentElement).getPropertyValue('--chart-series-1')`. A hex typed into the markup is a second copy that drifts, and the check fails it.
388: 
389: Which system to pick, what the roles mean and where the ceilings are: `color-system.md`.
390: 
391: ### The design-md delivery branch
392: 
393: A delivery generated from a local v3 `DESIGN.md` may carry `system=design-md` in both palette
394: sentinels. It remains a copy of its source form: the existing `chart-template` and
395: `chart-color-system` identity lines stay byte-identical, while the two palette blocks, the
396: provenance comments, the font declarations and the light corner ladder carry the reference's
397: projection. The block system is authoritative for this delivery branch, so it does not enter the
398: stock source-equality comparison or the catalog.
399: 
400: The provenance comment must be the first line after each begin marker and must carry the input path
401: as given to the applicator, a 64-hex SHA-256 of that `DESIGN.md`, and the applicator version. The
402: checker accepts the branch only when both comments are well formed and the inline `surface`, `ink`,
403: `muted`, `series-1` through `series-4` and `emphasis` values clear the same gates as the stock
404: systems on both grounds. A malformed comment or a failed inline gate is an error; there is no
405: force path and no source-equality exemption for a stock system.
406: 
407: ### The card reads as a product, not a template
408: 
409: Five rules from the polish pass, each held by the checker.
410: 
411: - **The source line is the source.** The visible `data-chart-part="source"` text names where the
412:   numbers came from and nothing else; the instruction that retargeting means replacing the data
413:   block lives in a comment directly above `CHART_DATA`. The `source-line` family errors when that
414:   instruction creeps back into the line a reader sees.
415: - **The plot is the largest thing on the card.** Cartesian forms draw in a 392-unit-high frame on
416:   the 720-unit width, about 54 percent, with the baseline, tick row and legend moved down with the
417:   frame. Forms whose shape does not fill a taller frame (calendar grid, heat matrix, unit grid and
418:   ring, treemap, progress, bullet, funnel, independent percentages, population pyramid) keep their
419:   own height; the reasoning per form is recorded with the pass.
420: - **The table folds, it never leaves.** The data table sits inside `<details class="data">` with a
421:   "Show the data" summary, open on every form, and keeps `data-chart-table` on the table itself
422:   so the accessibility and card-readout checks read it unchanged. It used to start closed wherever
423:   a tooltip answered the pointer, which left the tooltip as the only visible source of the values,
424:   one hover per number. The `table-disclosure` family holds the wrapper, the summary and the open
425:   state.
426: - **A finding declares its direction.** A `FINDING` block beside `READOUT` carries `trend` as
427:   `up`, `down` or `none` with a one-line reason; the footer draws a 12px inline arrow in the
428:   emphasis colour for up or down and nothing for none. A share, a comparison or a spread is
429:   `none`; only a change over time earns an arrow. The `finding-cue` family holds the block, the
430:   set and the read.
431: - **Numbers carry their unit and ticks stay short.** `READOUT.unit` is a short string, or empty
432:   when the card mixes units, printed after the value with a thin space; every tooltip form
433:   declares it. Axis ticks at or above five digits render through a hand-written `compact()` as
434:   `12k` or `1.2M` with one decimal at most, while the card and the table keep full digits, and
435:   `toLocaleString` and `Intl` stay forbidden.
436: 
437: ### A card may lead with its number
438: 
439: A form whose data has an honest baseline declares a `METRIC` block beside `READOUT` and prints a
440: value, a signed delta and the period above the plot. `present` is `true` or `false` in every form,
441: so the decision is written down rather than implied: twenty-five forms declare `false` because a
442: share, a distribution or a matrix has no earlier reading to compare against, and the block's own
443: `why` line says so.
444: 
445: - **The value is a literal.** `value` and `valueLabel` name a number the reader can find in the
446:   table; the delta is computed from the same data and never at draw time. A form that would have to
447:   invent either declares `present: false`.
448: - **The rung is published.** The value prints at the `metric` rung, 26px, which lives in the palette
449:   source beside the other roles, so the type-scale family accepts it without a template-local size.
450: - **The delta carries the same cue as the finding.** Up or down draws the 12px arrow, coloured by
451:   the emphasis role for a fall and the second series role for a rise, then the delta phrase and the
452:   period in muted text.
453: - **`present: false` means no element.** The `metric-block` family errors when a form declares the
454:   block absent and still ships the markup, and when a form ships the markup with no block at all.
455: 
456: ### The corner ladder rides in the same block
457: 
458: The light block carries one more kind of shared value: the five corner rungs, `--chart-radius-mark`
459: through `--chart-radius-card`. They are not colours and they live in their own object in the
460: palette source, but they are emitted into the same block because every file already carries that
461: block and the check already compares it against the source in both directions. They appear once
462: and only in that block, since a corner is the same corner on either ground. The rungs are the
463: measured ladder: 2px for a mark, 4.4px for a track, a swatch and the pill, 8.4px for the card
464: that holds the chart.
465: 
466: A corner is never typed into a file. A stylesheet reaches a rung the way it reaches a colour, and
467: SVG marks take theirs from CSS too: `rx` is a geometry property, so `.box { rx: var(--chart-radius-mark); }`
468: rounds a mark without a number appearing in the drawing code. Where a mark rounds only one end,
469: the drawing builds a path and reads the rung once through `getComputedStyle`, because an `rx`
470: rounds all four corners and a bar that meets a baseline should not round the end that meets it.
471: 
472: A corner computed from a mark's own geometry is not a rung and stays in the drawing code. The
473: range bars in `daily-range.html` are rounded to half their own width, which is a lozenge rather
474: than a shared value.

478: ## 7. THE TWENTY-FIVE RULES
479: 
480: Every rule below is enforced, and three are enforced in part. The check name is what appears in the
481: corpus check output, so a failure points at the rule it broke.
482: 
483: The three partial ones are named here rather than left for a reader to discover, because "every
484: rule is enforced" is the sentence that makes a green run mean something and it was doing work it
485: had not earned. Rule 10's table half is a substring test that a commented-out attribute satisfies.
486: Rule 13's settle time is not asserted at all: reading a duration out of a stylesheet says what the
487: author wrote, not when the picture stopped moving, and only the two-render comparison observes
488: that. Rule 14 asserts that the affordances are declared and never measures a rendered page.
489: Section 9 carries the full account of what a run does not observe.
490: 
491: | # | Rule | Check | The failure it prevents |
492: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
493: | 1 | Complete document: doctype, `lang`, charset, viewport, a non-empty title | `document-shape` | Shipping a fragment as a deliverable |
494: | 2 | Identity tag present, lower-case kebab, equal to the filename stem | `identity` | A file nothing can index |
495: | 3 | A stock colour system exists in the palette source, or a design-md delivery carries the provenance-gated branch | `identity`, `design-md` | A file pointing at a system nobody defined, or a themed copy with an untraceable palette |
496: | 4 | One palette block per theme, two at most, each matching its own stock projection, or a design-md block with provenance and inline gates | `palette-block`, `design-md` | Silent theme drift, invisible in a diff, or a themed block that bypasses the gates |
497: | 5 | No colour literal outside the palette block | `colour-literals` | A palette edit that reaches half the file |
498: | 6 | No remote resource and no runtime fetch | `no-external` | A chart that stops working away from the network |
499: | 7 | Every inline script compiles | `script-parses` | A file that throws on open, which no reading catches |
500: | 8 | Exactly one data block, before the drawing code | `data-block` | An editor hunting for the numbers through the rendering |
501: | 9 | Element ids unique in the file | `unique-ids` | Two charts silently rendering into one container |
502: | 10 | Every `svg` carries `role="img"` and an `aria-labelledby` that resolves, and the file carries a `data-chart-table` | `accessibility` | A screen reader getting nothing at all from the chart |

508: | 16 | An indexed data class carries the palette token of its own index, the indices run from one without a gap, and they stop at the declared system's capacity | `series-mapping` | An encoding quietly reversed or shuffled, agreeing with its own legend and with nothing else |
509: | 17 | A form that refuses the pointer says why, and cannot also carry a register that answers one | `interaction-hygiene` | A form claiming both that it needs no pointer and that it answers one, or an inert claim nobody can act on because it names no reason |
510: | 18 | Every number a card can show appears in the form's data table | `card-readout` | A hover that reveals a reading no other route reaches, which hides data from every reader not holding a pointer |
511: | 19 | Every form on disk has a row in the per-form pointer contract, and every row has a form | `pointer-contract-coverage` | A form shipping with no decision recorded about what a pointer does on it, or a row describing a form nobody ships |

518: 
519: Rule 4 used to say exactly one block, and it said so for a good reason: one block per file is one
520: place a colour can drift, and a diff shows it. A theme is the one thing that argument does not
521: survive, because a file that answers a dark system needs a second set of values and there is
522: nowhere else in a self-contained document to put them. So the ceiling moved from one to two and
523: stayed a ceiling. Two is every theme this corpus has, the check counts the regions rather than
524: trusting the count, and each region is matched against its own projection of the source in both
525: directions, which is the property the old rule was protecting.
526: 
527: Rule 13 carries a number, and the number is what makes rule 12 checkable. One second is the
528: settle time: every animation in the corpus finishes inside it, and the render check opens each
529: file with a three second budget, which is three times over. Without a stated settle time the two
530: rules argue with each other. Rule 12 wants a picture that does not change, rule 13 permits one
531: that changes for a while, and nobody can say when the second stopped being true. A named ceiling
532: turns that into arithmetic.
533: 
534: The three parts of rule 13 are one requirement, not three preferences. A fallback that shortens
535: the motion is not a fallback, because the reader who asked their system for no motion still gets
536: motion. An animation that repeats has no settled state at all, which breaks rule 12 by
537: construction rather than by accident. And a motion that outruns the render budget is caught
538: mid-move, which is the same failure as randomness: two renders disagree and nobody can tell which
539: one is the bug.
540: 
541: The settle time is a ceiling the file has to hold on its own, not a promise about the data it
542: shipped with. A stagger that adds a delay per mark would walk past one second the moment a reader
543: pastes thirty rows into the data block, so the delay is capped rather than accumulated. Nothing
544: about the ceiling depends on how many rows the file happens to carry.

546: Rule 14 is the one a desktop author never notices is missing. `width: 100%` on the drawing
547: looks correct at every size the author tries, and squashes the chart into illegibility at the
548: width most readers will open it on. A floor plus a pannable region is the whole fix, and it is
549: two declarations.
550: 
551: The rule reached half the card for a while, and the half it missed was the half that moved the
552: page. A card holds a drawing and a table, the drawing had somewhere to pan and the table did not,
553: so a table wider than the screen took the headline and the source line sideways with it. Measured
554: at 500 units, two files did that: the matrix form by 133 units and its delivery by 71. The table
555: region now pans the way the figure does. It declares no floor of its own, because a table already
556: has one: its cells cannot shrink below the text in them, which is the intrinsic minimum an SVG at
557: `width: 100%` does not have, and that is the whole reason the drawing needs a number and the table
558: does not.
559: 
560: Rule 15 is the one that only pays later. The corner was already identical in every form before
561: it was enforced, so the check found nothing wrong on the day it shipped. That is the point: the
562: uniformity held because twenty authors happened to agree, and a convention nothing asserts breaks
563: on the file nobody diffs closely.
564: 
565: Rule 10 is the one worth doing first rather than last. A title inside the vector output, an accessible role and a hidden data table cost almost nothing while a template is being written, and are close to unaffordable to retrofit across a whole corpus.
566: 
567: Rule 16 is the one that decides what the picture means, and it was the last one anything looked at.
568: Every other colour rule asks where a value came from. The palette block is matched against the
569: source in both directions, no literal may appear outside it, and the source itself is gated for
570: contrast and for the direction its ramp runs. A file that hands those tokens out in the wrong order
571: satisfies all of them. Reverse the five mappings in a matrix form and the darkest step now paints
572: the lowest reading; the legend reverses with it, because the legend is drawn from the same classes,
573: so the picture agrees with itself and disagrees with the data. What survives the permutation is
574: arithmetic rather than appearance, which is why the rule is stated as one: the number in the class
575: name and the number in the token it resolves to are the same number.
576: 
577: Rules 21 through 23 close the three seams that remain after that indexed check. A keyed series
578: declaration makes the semantic name and the paint answer the same question. A local readout block
579: makes a card's label, value and datum field inspectable where the data is edited. A curve declaration
580: makes interpolation a stated reading of the data rather than an implementation detail. Each is
581: checked against the file that carries it, and each fails on the first drift rather than relying on
582: a reviewer to notice a second copy.
583: 
584: ---
585: 
586: ## 8. AUTHORING A NEW TEMPLATE
587: 
588: 1. Find the question in `catalog.md`. If no row answers it, that is a gap to report rather than a chart to improvise.
589: 2. Copy `assets/style-reference/evilcharts/palette-sheet-neutral.html` to `assets/templates/<id>.html`.
590: 3. Set the identity tag and the title. The id, the filename stem and the catalog row all carry the same string.
591: 4. Choose the colour system, and paste both of its palette blocks from the corpus check output. The check prints the light block and the dark one, each against the block it expected to find.
592: 5. Replace the data block with the real shape, and write the drawing code below it.
593: 6. Write the headline as a conclusion.
594: 7. Add the catalog row.
595: 8. Run `node scripts/check-corpus.cjs --render` and read the `RESULT:` line.
596: 
597: When the check fails on a template, fix the template. A validator edited to accept a file it was right to reject is worth less than no validator, because the next reader believes it.
598: 
599: ---
600: 
601: ## 9. WHAT THE CHECK DOES NOT OBSERVE
602: 
603: Stated plainly, so nobody reads a green run as more than it is.
604: 
605: - **It does not look at the picture.** With `--render` it opens the file in a headless browser and confirms the figure region holds real elements after the script ran, which catches an empty box. It does not know whether the bars are the right height.
606: - **It does not read console warnings.** A script that throws is caught, because the marks never appear. A script that warns is not.
607: - **It does not judge the headline.** Whether the top line states a conclusion is a review question.
608: - **Without `--render` it has not opened anything.** The summary line says so on every run. A structural pass is not a rendering pass.
609: - **It does not watch the motion.** With `--render` it opens each file twice after the settle time and confirms the two documents are identical, which catches a picture that is still changing when the review screenshots it. It does not see the animation itself, so whether the wipe reads as an entrance is a review question.
610: - **It does not measure a narrow screen.** Rule 14 is asserted from the stylesheet, not from a rendered page, because a headless browser hands back the DOM and the DOM does not say whether the page overflowed. The check proves both pan affordances are declared and that the drawing's floor is not above its natural width. Whether the chart is legible at that floor is a review question, and the floor itself is a judgement nobody has measured per form. A page that overflows sideways is measurable, but only by injecting a script into a copy of the file and reading `scrollWidth` back, which is a review step rather than a corpus check.
611: - **It does not judge either theme by eye.** With `--render` it opens each file with the colour scheme pinned light, twice, and again with the scheme pinned dark, and it asserts that the dark open paints a different picture from the light one. That proves the second block reaches the paint rather than merely sitting in the file, which no reading of the text can prove. It says nothing about whether the dark values are the right ones, and it forces the preference with a browser flag rather than reading an operating system, so what a particular reader's machine resolves is still a question for a real browser.
612: - **It does not point at anything.** Both opens are made with no pointer input, which is exactly what makes them a fair test of the settled picture and exactly what leaves most of section 10 to be walked by hand. Whether a card opens on the right mark, whether it flips at an edge and whether a key entry latches are all read by a person. What a pointer-free run can see is the state a file ships in, and that half is now asserted: `interaction-state` fails a drawing that opens already dimmed or with a card already filled, neither of which a settled comparison would catch, because both opens agree with each other exactly as a correct file's do.
613: 
614: ---
615: 
616: ## 10. WHAT A FILE MAY DO WITH A POINTER
617: 
618: This contract binds every rendered chart artifact this skill ships: the forms under
619: `assets/templates/`, and any delivery made from one. A delivery inherits its parent template's
620: contract, and it does not get to answer the pointer differently just because it is a themed or
621: retargeted copy rather than a template.
622: 
623: That inheritance is a state the corpus is in, not an aspiration, and it is stated so a reader can
624: disagree with it by opening the files. Every delivery's pointer contract matches its own parent
625: template's, mechanism for mechanism: a delivery whose parent carries the hover card carries the
626: same card, the same listeners and the same hygiene line, adapted to the delivery's own marks and
627: data, and a delivery whose parent is inert declares `data-chart-inert` with the parent's own reason
628: string, copied rather than restated. The packet ships no deliveries of its own; the rule binds the
629: ones the applicator writes and the ones a user retargets. A delivery found behind its parent is a
630: defect in the delivery, the same way a drifted palette block is, and the fix is to bring the
631: delivery forward, never to excuse it.
632: 
633: A chart answers a pointer. Eighteen forms carry the hover-card register today. The other forms either
634: print their values in the drawing or carry a native title on a mark, so a card would repeat the
635: reading. See the per-form table below for the decided contract of all 29 forms.
636: 
637: The pointer rows remain a register for behaviour a static check cannot see, while the state,
638: number-format and card/table boundaries are asserted. The split is marked here so nobody reads a
639: green run as agreement with the whole section.
640: 
641: `interaction-hygiene` requires the hygiene line in any file whose markup declares one of the three registers, and separately fails an unconditional `outline: none` on a focus and any `user-select: none`, which are the two ways the line could be widened into taking something away from a reader. `interaction-state` requires the dim attribute to ship empty and the tooltip group to ship without content. `number-format` fails any host-locale formatter anywhere in the corpus, and requires a file carrying a hover card to define its `READOUT` block and read its key from the registered datum.
642: 
643: Everything else here is unasserted. What a handler may do, where a card flips, whether a figure inside a card is also in the table, and whether a selection latches are all read by a person.
644: 
645: ### The four registers
646: 
647: | Attribute | Where it goes | What it means |
648: | --- | --- | --- |
649: | `data-chart-tooltip` | a positioned HTML element inside the figure | The form carries a hover card. The element is declared empty, filled from `READOUT`, and raised above the marks without painting tooltip text in SVG |
650: | `data-chart-legend` | an HTML row below the plot inside the figure | The form carries its key inside the figure. Each entry is a button, because the key is also the control for the dim |
651: | `data-chart-dim` | the `svg` element | The form can hold one series against the rest. The attribute is empty until a reader asks, and the series index fills it |
652: | `data-chart-inert` | the chart's figure wrapper (the `<div class="figure" data-chart-part="figure">` element, not a literal `<figure>` tag) | The form correctly answers a pointer with nothing. The attribute's value is the reason, and an empty or whitespace-only value fails the check |
653: 
654: A form that gains any of the three also carries one line of interaction hygiene: `:focus:not(:focus-visible) { outline: none; }`. That drops the focus ring for a reader who clicked and keeps it for a reader who tabbed. Text stays selectable. A delivered chart is a document, and the numbers in it are meant to be copied out.

15: # Chart Template Contract
16: 
17: A template is one HTML file. It opens on a double click, with no install, no package manager and no build step, and it keeps working when the person who received it edits the numbers by hand.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: Both of those properties are load-bearing. The reader is a writer or an operations analyst rather than a developer, and the file has to survive being emailed to somebody who will open it on a laptop with no network.
24: 
25: ---
26: 
27: ## 2. THE DELIVERY UNIT
28: 
29: One file holds one chart. Inside it, the visible unit is a card with five parts in a fixed order.
30: 
31: | Part | Marker | What goes in it |
32: | --- | --- | --- |
33: | Headline | `data-chart-part="headline"` | A conclusion, not a chart type. "Revenue by plan" is a label. "Where we gained and where we bled" is an argument |
34: | Subtitle | `data-chart-part="subtitle"` | The legend and the time range, in a sentence |
35: | Figure | `data-chart-part="figure"` | The drawing itself |
36: | Footer | `data-chart-part="footer"` | The one-line finding in ink, separated from the figure by the rule |
37: | Source | `data-chart-part="source"` | The muted description line in the footer; where the numbers came from |
38: 
39: The fixed five are what make a chart legible with no caption around it. The headline rule is the highest-value writing rule in this packet: a reader who takes nothing but the top line should still have learned something. The footer is part of the card rather than a caption added around it: the finding tells the reader what to notice, and the source stays attached to that reading.
40: 
41: ### Gallery and delivery are different things
42: 
43: A delivery is one card in one file, and it is what reaches a user. A gallery is many cards on one page, used as a workbench for finding a form. Never hand over a gallery. It carries every other chart's demo data with the user's one real chart somewhere inside it.
44: 
45: ---
46: 
47: ## 3. THE FILE SKELETON
48: 
49: Copy the skeleton from `assets/style-reference/evilcharts/palette-sheet-neutral.html`, which is a working file that passes every check. The structure is:
50: 
51: ```
52: <!doctype html>
53: <html lang="en">
54: <head>
55:   <meta charset>, <meta name="viewport">, <title>
56:   <meta name="chart-template"     content="<id>">
57:   <meta name="chart-color-system" content="<system>">
58:   <style>
59:     /* CHART_PALETTE:BEGIN system=<system> */
60:     /* DESIGN.md provenance: path=<local path> sha256=<64 hex> generator=<version> */
61:     :root { every colour role and every corner rung, pasted from the palette source }
62:     /* CHART_PALETTE:END */
63: 
64:     /* CHART_PALETTE_DARK:BEGIN system=<system> */
65:     /* DESIGN.md provenance: path=<local path> sha256=<64 hex> generator=<version> */
66:     @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
67:       :root { every colour role again, pasted from the same source's dark values }
68:     }
69:     /* CHART_PALETTE_DARK:END */
70: 
71:     everything else, referring only to var(--chart-…)
72:   </style>
73: </head>
74: <body>
75:   the card: headline, subtitle, figure, footer with finding and source
76:   a table carrying data-chart-table
77:   <script>
78:     /* CHART_DATA:BEGIN */
79:     the numbers, and nothing else
80:     /* CHART_DATA:END */
81: 
82:     /* CHART_SERIES:BEGIN */
83:     one object per named series: key, label, token and paint classes
84:     /* CHART_SERIES:END */
85: 
86:     /* READOUT:BEGIN */
87:     label formatter, value formatter and datum-field key for a card-bearing form
88:     /* READOUT:END */
89: 
90:     /* CURVE:BEGIN */
91:     const CURVE = 'linear' | 'step' | 'monotone', with one-line rationale
92:     /* CURVE:END */
93: 
94:     the drawing code
95:   </script>
96: </body>
97: </html>
98: ```
99: 
100: The sentinels are how the corpus check finds the two palette regions it has an opinion about. Do not rename them, and use each pair once. The dark pair carries its own name for that reason: a second block under the light block's name would be the same sentinel twice, and then nothing can say which region a drifted value came from.
101: 
102: ### The type scale, as the compact card register
103: 
104: The visual pass moves the corpus to the compact register in the frozen shadcn examples: a title
105: that is easy to scan, a description that stays secondary, and 12px figure labels that remain
106: legible beside a data mark. The palette source publishes the projection under `typeScale`, the
107: `type-scale` family reads it from there, and a size outside it fails rather than becoming a
108: one-off guess. The two palette proof sheets keep their finer six-rung scale under `sheetRoles`.
109: 
110: | Role | Size | What is set in it |
111: | --- | --- | --- |
112: | headline | 16px | The card title, semibold and ink coloured |
113: | body | 14px | The page default and the card description |
114: | label/tick/note | 12px | Axis ticks, footer labels, tooltip rows, legend labels and compact in-figure notes |
115: | month strip | 10px | A month name in the calendar grid, where the year leaves a narrow strip |
116: | hero | 56px | The single headline number in `progress-single` |
117: | ring total | 34px | The total at the centre of `unit-ring` |
118: 
119: The values are measured from the frozen shadcn copy: the card header keeps title and description
120: together (`chart-area-interactive.tsx:157-164`), Cartesian labels use the compact chart text
121: register (`chart.tsx:63-69`), and the footer uses `text-sm`, `font-medium` and a muted second row
122: (`chart-line-linear.tsx:78-84`). The standalone files express those roles in CSS rather than in
123: Tailwind utilities, but the scale is the same decision.
124: 
125: The two departures remain deliberate. `progress-single` prints its hero figure at 56px and
126: `unit-ring` prints its ring total at 34px because each is the point of the chart rather than a
127: label on it. `calendar-grid` keeps its 10px month strip because a year of days leaves no room for
128: the full label rung.
129: 
130: ### The shadcn visual register
131: 
132: The corpus keeps the shadcn choices that survive the standalone-file constraint. The frozen line
133: examples remove both axis and tick lines, leave an 8px tick margin, draw a 2px line and turn point
134: dots off (`chart-line-default.tsx:56-74`). The frozen area examples are our measurement of what
135: shadcn ships: a vertical 0.8-to-0.1 gradient with 0.4 flat opacity for stacked areas
136: (`chart-area-gradient.tsx:72-112`), from which ours derive — the shipped single-area fade runs
137: 0.35 to 0.04 (`daily-line.html:137-138`) and the shipped stacked bands sit at 0.4 flat. The frozen
138: tooltip content uses a bordered, rounded, padded, shadowed card with muted labels and mono values
139: (`chart.tsx:190-259`), while the legend uses 8px squares with 2px corners and a 16px row gap
140: (`chart.tsx:290-322`).
141: 
142: The HTML projection is deliberately local: `--chart-surface`, `--chart-rule`, `--chart-muted`,
143: and the series tokens supply all paint; the card is positioned inside `.figure`; and the card reads
144: the form's `READOUT` block. The tooltip is never an SVG text layer. A keyed multi-series form gets
145: one centered HTML legend row below the plot, generated from `CHART_SERIES`, with one button chip per key.
146: 
147: Cartesian single-series forms use the first categorical series token for their primary mark. The
148: emphasis token is reserved for the highlighted mark. Unit grids, rings, ordered ramps and other
149: non-Cartesian forms keep their existing colour logic because their colour is carrying a different
150: question.
151: 
152: ### The geometry defaults ride beside the palette block
153: 
154: Every file carries one `GEOMETRY DEFAULTS` block, immediately after its dark palette block. It
155: records the five measurements every file in the corpus shares: the 720-unit drawing frame, the
156: pan floor, the card width, the card padding and the page padding.
157: 
158: The block is a written record rather than an indirection, and that is forced rather than chosen.
159: Neither place these numbers are used can read a custom property. A `viewBox` attribute takes a
160: number, and rule 14's floor is read out of the stylesheet as a literal by the check that
161: enforces it, so a `min-width` resolving through a variable would fail the rule it satisfies.
162: 
163: What the block deliberately does not carry is the frame height or the four plot insets. Those
164: are per-form, because a left inset is sized to the widest label a form actually carries, and
165: copying one form's inset into another buys uniformity by cutting a label off. A form that
166: departs from a shared value says why beside the value it uses instead.
167: 
168: `geometry-block` asserts it. Every chart form and every proof sheet has to carry the block and
169: every copy has to match the others byte for byte. The set is derived from the two directories
170: rather than listed, so a new form joins it by existing rather than by being remembered, and a
171: corpus where the block had been scattered over some files would fail rather than pass a count.
172: 
173: ---
174: 
175: ## 4. HOW IT RECEIVES DATA
176: 
177: One named array at the top of the inline script, between the `CHART_DATA` sentinels, and everything below it renders. That is the whole contract, and it is the right one, because the person editing a delivered file is looking for the numbers and nothing else.
178: 
179: The data block holds literal values. It never fetches, never computes the numbers it is displaying and never reads the clock. A chart that changes on its own cannot be reviewed, because two screenshots of one file disagree and nobody can tell which is the bug.
180: 
181: ### The one exception, named
182: 
183: Two forms compute a value they display, and both are deliberate: the waterfall's closing
184: total and the stacked area's per-period total. Neither invents a number. Each is the sum
185: of values the reader can already see, computed beside them and auditable against them, and
186: in both cases typing the total by hand would create a second copy that drifts the first
187: time a step is edited.
188: 
189: That is the whole exception and it does not generalise. A computed value is allowed when it
190: is a total of the typed values, sits next to them, and would otherwise be a hand-kept
191: duplicate. Everything else belongs upstream, in the workbook or query the numbers came
192: from. That covers a rate, a share of an untyped denominator, a smoothed series, and any
193: value derived from another source. The test is whether a reader holding only the data block can check the figure. If
194: they cannot, the file is computing rather than displaying.
195: 
196: Everything else the drawing code derives is geometry or presentation, not data: an axis
197: ceiling, a tick ladder, a bar height, a formatted label. Those are how the numbers are
198: drawn, and they are not what this clause is about.
199: 
200: ### A named series owns one token
201: 
202: When a form carries more than one named stream, the streams sit in one `CHART_SERIES` block
203: beside `CHART_DATA`. Each object has a stable `key`, the label a reader sees, exactly one
204: `--chart-series-N` token and the CSS classes that paint that stream. The declaration is the one
205: source for the name-to-paint relationship; the index is still the position used by the data array,
206: but it is not allowed to become a second mapping kept somewhere else in the file.
207: 
208: The keyed forms are `bar-line-composed`, `grouped-bars`, `parallel-axes`, `population-pyramid`,
209: `stacked-area` and `stacked-bars`. `series-mapping` checks both sides: an entry with no token or
210: more than one token fails, and a class whose paint does not match its key fails. Ordered colour
211: steps, sign classes and other categorical ladders keep their existing indexed contract; they are
212: not named series merely because they use more than one colour.
213: 
214: ### A card carries its readout knobs
215: 
216: Every form with `data-chart-tooltip` carries one `READOUT` block beside its data. The block owns
217: three local decisions: `label` formats the card's labels, `value` formats its values and `key`
218: names the property of the datum passed to card registration that supplies the card's label. The
219: registration path reads the label as `READOUT.label(datum[READOUT.key])`. When a displayed label is
220: computed or the registration has no existing row object, the caller passes a small record with a
221: literal property matching `key`. The value formatter may preserve a value already rendered by the
222: form's fixed-comma `fmt`, which keeps derived strings such as a signed change readable while still
223: giving the card one local knob.
224: 
225: `number-format` asserts the block and its use. A tooltip without `READOUT`, a block without all
226: three fields, a card path that does not read `READOUT.label`, `READOUT.value` and
227: `READOUT.key` from the registered datum, or a path that builds an object with `[READOUT.key]` only
228: to read that same property back is an error.
229: 
230: ### A time path states its curve
231: 
232: Any form that draws a path over time declares one `CURVE` block beside its data. The value is one
233: of `linear`, `step` or `monotone`, and a one-line rationale sits beside it. `linear` is the
234: default for measured trends because it connects the observations without adding a shape they did
235: not record. `step` is for discrete states. `monotone` is for a series whose meaning has been
236: reviewed and whose smooth path must not overshoot its observations. `natural` is not a contract
237: value: it adds curvature without saying what the data means.
238: 
239: The path builder reads `CURVE` when it assembles its `d` attribute, so changing the declaration
240: changes the construction rather than only the prose around it. `curve-contract` checks the
241: sentinel, the allowed set, the rationale and the read by the path. The current time-path forms
242: are `bar-line-composed`, `daily-line`, `stacked-area` and the `orders-after-the-price-change`
243: delivery; each ships `linear` because each is a measured trend with finite gaps left visible.
244: 
245: ### A form declares what its marks do
246: 
247: Whether a figure adds dots, how it fills the space under a line, and whether its zero means
248: anything are decisions the paint code makes either way. A `MARKS` block beside the data states
249: them in words a check can hold against the paint: `points` is `none`, `sparse` or `all`; `fill` is
250: `none`, `gradient` or `flat`; `zero` is `baseline` or `meaningful`. A one-line why sits beside
251: them, and it is the only prose in the block, because a longer reading of the drawing is the second
252: description that goes stale first.
253: 
254: `sparse` marks the readings the sentence cites and nothing else, which is why `daily-line` and
255: `spark` carry one dot each rather than twenty-eight. `all` belongs to the forms whose reading *is*
256: the point: `scatter`, `dumbbell`, `distribution-strip` and `parallel-axes`. `meaningful` is
257: declared by one form, `waterfall`, because its steps are signed and its baseline separates a rise
258: from a fall. Every other form's zero is the floor its bars stand on.
259: 
260: The `mark-policy` family holds each word against the drawing, not just against the vocabulary. A
261: declared fade needs a gradient and a declared flat fill needs an opacity, and neither accepts the
262: other's paint. A zero is meaningful exactly when a reading falls below it. Points are held one way
263: only: a form promising marks has to draw them, while a form declaring `none` may still carry a
264: circle, because several forms place an invisible one purely as something a pointer can reach.
265: 
266: ### A level a reader measures against is declared
267: 
268: A target, an average or a threshold drawn across a plot is a claim about the data, not decoration,
269: so a form that can carry one says whether it does. Every form built on the corpus's one vertical
270: value scale and a drawn grid declares a `REFERENCE` list of `{ value, label, why }`; an empty list
271: draws nothing, and the drawing takes all three fields from the block rather than from a data field
272: of its own.
273: 
274: That set is narrower than "cartesian", deliberately. A form reading two scales at once cannot say
275: which one a chart-wide value belongs to, which rules out `bar-line-composed`. A form whose value
276: runs along the horizontal, or whose points each answer to their own axis, has no single level to
277: draw, which rules out `pick-times-by-depot` and `parallel-axes`. `spark` has the scale and no axis,
278: no labels and no grid, so a named rule across it would break the form. The line is dashed at the ink
279: colour so it is not mistaken for the grid, and its label is set at the right edge of the plot, above
280: the rule.
281: 
282: Two forms carry a line, and both carry it for the same reason: the headline is a claim about a
283: level, and the level is already in the data. `daily-line` declares the first week's average, which
284: nothing after day eleven reaches. The `orders-after-the-price-change` delivery declares the ten
285: days before the change, 184 against 140 after it, which is the "almost a quarter lower" its
286: headline states. The `reference-line` family holds the block, the three fields, the read by the
287: drawing, that the drawing appends a rule, and that the file styles it.
288: 
289: `bullet` is not a consumer, and the reason is worth stating because it looks like one. Its target
290: is per row, not per plot: four measures carry four different targets against four different scales,
291: and a chart-wide list cannot express that. Its target stays in its data.
292: 
293: ### When a form cannot honour the data it was given
294: 
295: A form is honest inside a documented shape, and two different things set that shape. The catalog
296: states how much data a form can carry: `scatter` past twenty points and `heat-matrix` past a
297: hundred cells each grow the frame and print one line naming the count and the ceiling. The palette
298: states how many colours a form has to give out, which is a harder ceiling because the file cannot
299: paint past it at all: `unit-ring`, `unit-grid`, `stacked-bars`, `treemap` and `stacked-area` each
300: draw the marks past that ceiling outside the encoding, in the rule colour, and print the same kind
301: of line. Seven forms in total.
302: 
303: The colour ceiling is worth stating separately, because reaching past it used to fail silently and
304: loudly at the same time. A class the stylesheet defines no fill for is not an unstyled mark; it is
305: a black one, because black is what an SVG paints when nothing says otherwise. So the group the
306: encoding could not carry came out as the strongest mark on the page, under a key that never named
307: it. Nothing in a green run said so.
308: 
309: A missing reading gets the same treatment: `bar-line-composed`, `daily-line`, `daily-range` and
310: `stacked-area` break the mark at the gap rather than drawing through it, and print how many
311: readings were left out.
312: 
313: A notice belongs in the figure when a reader looking at the picture would otherwise draw a
314: wrong conclusion from it, and it is not spread across every form for its own sake. A console
315: warning was the alternative and was rejected: the person the ceiling protects is reading a
316: chart, not a developer console.
317: 
318: ### An empty data block says so, on every form and every delivery
319: 
320: All twenty-nine forms carry the same guard, marked `CHART_EMPTY_NOTICE`,
321: above their drawing code. When the data block holds nothing readable, the file prints one line in
322: the middle of the frame and draws nothing else.
323: 
324: The deliveries carried no guard at all until the ground for exempting them was read rather than
325: repeated. The exemption said a delivery carries the notice of the form it was built from, and none
326: of the six did. A delivery is also the copy somebody edits, which makes it the copy most likely to
327: be handed an empty block. The only file this does not reach is a proof sheet, whose data block is
328: the palette it draws rather than a reading it displays.
329: 
330: This is the clearest case the rule above describes rather than a new rule. An empty frame and a
331: chart whose values are all zero look identical, so a reader shown an empty box has no way to
332: tell which one they are holding. The notice tells them.
333: 
334: Readability is what the guard tests, not length. A block whose entries all carry values that are
335: not finite numbers has length and still has nothing to draw, so it fires. One row does not fire
336: it. That distinction matters more than it looks: a guard written against `length` alone passes an
337: array of nulls straight through to a drawing that has nothing to draw, and a guard that coerces
338: before it tests reads `null` as zero and calls it a reading. The corpus already had the right
339: test, in the three time forms that break a line at a gap, and this guard uses the same one.
340: 
341: The notice is a text element inside the drawing, so a screen reader reaches it exactly as it
342: reaches the ceiling notices. Its wording is fixed rather than assembled from the data block, so
343: nothing a reader pastes into the file can reach the picture as text.
344: 
345: `empty-notice` asserts it on every run, and it asserts more than the sentinel. The guard has to
346: sit below the data block it reads, because a guard above it tests a name that is not defined yet,
347: and it has to carry the labelled block and the break that let it stop the drawing. A guard that
348: prints the notice and then draws anyway prints it over an empty frame, which is the picture the
349: notice exists to prevent.
